blocks.text: I can use reflexive pronouns with reflexive verbs, and understand that some verbs need prepositions to link them to a noun.
You will also learn to pronounce [g] correctly.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: Replaces the object in a sentence using a reflexive verb, e.g. ‘myself’.
A word that is used before a noun, a noun phrase, or a pronoun, connecting it to another word.

slides.title: [g] at the start and in the middle

blocks.text: The sound [g] usually makes a hard sound at the start and in the middle of words, like the ‘g’ in English ‘go’.
Be careful with cognates like ‘Region’. In English, ‘g’ is a soft ‘j’ sound after ‘i’ or ‘e’. The [g] in German is hard!

slides.title: [g] at the end of a syllable

blocks.text: If [g] is the final sound in a syllable, it sounds more like ‘k’, as in ‘Flugzeug’. The vocal cords don’t vibrate.

items: Ber{g}
Zu{g}
We{g} (way, path)
Erfol{g} (success)
Flu{g}zeu{g}

blocks.text: Compare: in ‘Frage’ (question) and ‘Geschichte’ (history) the [g] is at the start or in the middle of a syllable, so it is hard like in ‘go’.

items.q: In which word does the g sound more like ‘k’?
Which word starts with a hard [g], like in English ‘go’?
How is the g in ‘Region’ pronounced in German?

blocks.text: Tap each word to see what it means.
Use verbs reflexively when the subject and object of an action are the same. A reflexive pronoun is used in place of an object.

items: Ich ziehe die Jacke an. (I put on the jacket.)
Ich ziehe {mich} an. (I dress myself.)

blocks.text: When we use verbs reflexively, sometimes the meaning changes slightly. Often English uses a different verb for the reflexive and non-reflexive meanings.
A reflexive pronoun is used instead of an object when the subject is also affected by the action of the verb. The singular reflexive pronouns are:

items: Ich fühle mich wohl. (I feel well.)
Er fühlt sich müde.
Ich setze mich auf den Boden. (I sit on the ground.)

blocks.text: Mich and dich can be reflexive pronouns or direct object pronouns. Context tells us which!

items: Ich frage {dich}! (I am asking you: ‘dich’ is a direct object pronoun.)
Du setzt {dich} auf den Stuhl! (you are sitting yourself on the chair: reflexive, because the subject and the pronoun both refer to ‘you’.)

blocks.label: How can I tell?
blocks.text: Ask: does the pronoun refer to the same person as the subject? In ‘Ich wasche mich’ (I wash myself) it does, so it is reflexive.

blocks.q: Is the sentence reflexive or not?

items.text: Du setzt dich auf den Stuhl!
Ich freue mich auf den Austausch!

items.q: Ich interessiere ___ für die Schule in Schottland.

blocks.text: Some verbs that are used reflexively in German are not used the same way in English.

items: Use the reflexive verb ‘sich fühlen’ for internal emotions: Ich fühle mich wohl.
Use ‘spüren’ rather than ‘fühlen’ when describing external sensations: Sie spürt den Druck. (She feels the pressure.)

blocks.q: Which is the best way to say ‘She feels the pressure’?
blocks.why: The pressure is an external sensation, so German uses ‘spüren’ rather than ‘fühlen’.

blocks.text: Some verbs need a preposition to link them to a noun.

items: Ich warte auf das Buch. (I’m waiting for the book.)
Ich hoffe auf die Ferien. (I’m hoping for the holidays.)

blocks.text: Many verbs in German and English are followed directly by a noun: Ich halte das Buch. (I hold the book.)

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: German verbs often use different prepositions from those used in English. For example, ‘ich hoffe auf’ means ‘I’m hoping for’ (not ‘hoping on’).
In, auf, an and vor take the accusative case when describing movement, and the dative case when describing location.

items: Ich bin in der Stadt. (location: dative)
Ich gehe in die Stadt. (movement: accusative)

blocks.q: How do you say ‘I’m going into town’?
blocks.why: Going into town is movement, so ‘in’ takes the accusative: in die Stadt. ‘In der Stadt’ describes a location: ‘I’m in town’.

blocks.q: Choose the preposition that goes with the verb.

items.q: In English we say ‘to take part in’. In German: Ich nehme ___ dem Austausch teil.

items: At the start or in the middle of words, [g] is usually pronounced like the ‘g’ in English ‘go’. When [g] is the final sound in a syllable, it sounds like ‘k’, as in ‘Flugzeug’.
A reflexive pronoun is used instead of an object when the subject is also affected by the action of the verb, e.g. ‘ich wasche mich’.
Reflexive verbs need reflexive pronouns, which replace the object in the sentence.
Some verbs need prepositions to link them to a noun, for example ‘sich freuen auf’. German often uses different prepositions from English.

flashcards.front: How is [g] usually pronounced at the start or in the middle of a word?
How does [g] sound when it is the final sound in a syllable?
Is the g in ‘Region’ hard or soft in German?
flashcards.back: Hard, like in ‘go’ (not a soft ‘j’ as in English).

flashcards.front: When do we use a verb reflexively?
flashcards.back: When the subject and object of the action are the same.

flashcards.front: What does a reflexive pronoun do?
flashcards.back: It replaces the object in a sentence with a reflexive verb, e.g. ‘myself’.

flashcards.front: What are the singular reflexive pronouns?
What is the difference between ‘Ich ziehe die Jacke an’ and ‘Ich ziehe mich an’?
flashcards.back: ‘I put on the jacket’ and ‘I dress myself’. The reflexive pronoun replaces the object and the meaning changes slightly.

flashcards.front: Can ‘mich’ and ‘dich’ be something other than reflexive pronouns?
flashcards.back:
Yes, they can also be direct object pronouns. Context tells us which.

Ich frage dich! = I am asking you.

flashcards.front: Which verb is used for internal emotions: ‘spüren’ or ‘sich fühlen’?
flashcards.back:
sich fühlen.

Ich fühle mich wohl.

flashcards.front: Which verb is used for external sensations: ‘spüren’ or ‘fühlen’?
Say in German: ‘to hope for’ and ‘to wait for’ (verb + preposition)
Do German verbs always use the same prepositions as English verbs?
flashcards.back: No. They often use different ones, e.g. ‘ich hoffe auf’ = I’m hoping for (not ‘hoping on’).

flashcards.front: Which cases do in, auf, an and vor take for movement and for location?
flashcards.back:
Movement: accusative. Location: dative.

Ich gehe in die Stadt. / Ich bin in der Stadt.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: A school exchange: verbs with ‘an’, ‘auf’, ‘für’, ‘vor’, reflexive verbs
worksheet.instructions: Write the missing word, or answer the question. Use what you learnt about [g], reflexive pronouns and verbs with prepositions.

questions.prompt: Task A: Give the plural of ‘das Werkzeug’ (tool).
Task A: Give the plural of ‘das Spielzeug’ (toy).
Task A: Give the plural of ‘das Flugzeug’ (aeroplane).
Task A: In ‘Erfolg’ (success), the [g] is the final sound in the word. Which sound does it make: [g] as in ‘go’ or [k]?
questions.explanation: When [g] is the final sound in a syllable, it sounds more like ‘k’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Fühlst du ___ glücklich? Write mich or dich.
questions.explanation: The subject is ‘du’, so the reflexive pronoun is ‘dich’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Ich ziehe ___ schon um 6 Uhr an. Write mich or dich.
questions.explanation: The subject is ‘ich’, so the reflexive pronoun is ‘mich’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Du nennst ___ Wolf statt Wolfgang, nicht wahr? Write mich or dich.
questions.explanation: The subject is ‘du’, so the reflexive pronoun is ‘dich’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Er fühlt ___ müde. Write mich, dich or sich.
questions.explanation: The subject is ‘er’, so the reflexive pronoun is ‘sich’.

questions.prompt: Task B: Ich wasche ___ meine Tasche. Write mich, dich or nothing.
questions.explanation: The object is ‘meine Tasche’, so no reflexive pronoun is needed.

questions.prompt: Task C: Wolfgang hofft trotzdem ___ gutes Wetter. Write the missing preposition.
Task C: Alastair hat ___ schlechtem Wetter gewarnt. Write the missing preposition.
Task C: Wolfgang interessiert sich ___ die Landschaft. Write the missing preposition.
questions.explanation: ‘Sich interessieren für’ means ‘to be interested in’.
